entities.summary: The 1955 system , also known as the one-and-a-half party system, is a term used by scholars to describe the dominant-party system that has existed in Japan since 1955, in which the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) has held by itself or in coalition with Komeito a government nearly uninterrupted, with opposition parties largely incapable of forming significant or long lasting alternatives, other than for brief stints in 1993–1994 and 2009–2012. The terms 1955 system and the one-and-a-half party system are credited to Junnosuke Masumi, who described the 1955 system as "a grand political dam into which the history of Japanese politics surge".

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The 1955 system has had a significant impact on Japan's political landscape, limiting the ability of opposition parties to form lasting alternatives and shaping the country's party politics for decades. Its influence can be seen in the prolonged dominance of the Liberal Democratic Party.
